label: Phaedo · The Philosopher's Death
title: The Philosopher's Death
paragraphs: ECHECRATES: Were you there yourself, Phaedo, with Socrates on the day he drank the poison in the prison, or did you hear of it from someone else?
PHAEDO: I was there myself, Echecrates.

ECHECRATES: Then what were the things the man said before his death? And how did he die? I would gladly hear it. For none of the citizens of Phlius goes to Athens much at all these days, and no visitor has come from there in a long time who was able to give us any clear report about these things, except just that he drank poison and died; of the rest he had nothing to tell.
PHAEDO: Then you did not learn about the trial either, and how it went?
ECHECRATES: Yes, someone did report that to us, and we wondered that, though it took place long before, he evidently died much later. Why was that, Phaedo?
PHAEDO: It came about by chance, Echecrates. It happened that on the day before the trial the stern of the ship that the Athenians send to Delos had been wreathed.
ECHECRATES: And what ship is that?

PHAEDO: That is the ship, as the Athenians say, in which Theseus once went off to Crete taking those twice seven, and saved them and was saved himself. So they made a vow to Apollo then, as it is told, that if they were saved they would send a mission to Delos every year; and they have sent it to the god year by year ever since, and still do now. Once they have begun the mission, it is their law to keep the city pure during that time and to put no one to death in the city's name until the ship has reached Delos and come back here again; and this sometimes takes a long time, when the winds happen to hold them back. The mission begins when the priest of Apollo wreathes the stern of the ship; and this happened, as I say, on the day before the trial. That is why Socrates had a long time in the prison between the trial and his death.

ECHECRATES: And what about the death itself, Phaedo? What was said and done, and which of the man's friends were with him? Or did the officials not allow them to be present, so that he died alone, without friends?
PHAEDO: Not at all. Some were there — many, in fact.
ECHECRATES: Then do your best to report all of this to us as clearly as you can, unless you happen to be busy.
PHAEDO: No, I am free, and I will try to tell you the story. For to remember Socrates, whether I speak of him myself or listen to someone else, is always the sweetest thing of all to me.
ECHECRATES: Well, Phaedo, those who are going to listen to you are of just the same mind. So try to go through everything as exactly as you can.

PHAEDO: For my part, what I felt when I was there was astonishing. No pity came over me, as at being present at the death of a man who was my friend; for the man seemed to me happy, Echecrates, both in his manner and in his words, so fearlessly and nobly did he meet his end. So it came to me that even in going to Hades he was not going without a divine dispensation, and that when he arrived there he would fare well, if anyone ever did. For these reasons hardly any feeling of pity came over me, as would seem natural for someone present at a time of mourning; nor again pleasure, as when we were engaged in philosophy in our usual way — for the talk was of that kind — but simply a strange feeling was on me, an unfamiliar mixture, blended of pleasure and of pain together, as I reflected that in a little while he was going to die. And all of us who were there were in much the same state, now laughing, now weeping, and one of us more than the rest, Apollodorus — you know the man, I think, and his manner.
ECHECRATES: Of course.
PHAEDO: Well, he was entirely in that state, and I was shaken myself, and so were the others.
ECHECRATES: And who were there, Phaedo?

PHAEDO: Of the local men, this Apollodorus was there, and Critobulus and his father, and also Hermogenes and Epigenes and Aeschines and Antisthenes. Ctesippus of Paeania was there too, and Menexenus, and some other local men. Plato, I think, was ill.
ECHECRATES: Were any foreigners there?
PHAEDO: Yes: Simmias of Thebes, and Cebes and Phaedondes; and from Megara, Euclides and Terpsion.
ECHECRATES: What about Aristippus and Cleombrotus? Were they there?
PHAEDO: No, they were not; they were said to be in Aegina.
ECHECRATES: Was anyone else there?
PHAEDO: I think those were about all who were there.
ECHECRATES: Well then, what do you say the talk was?

PHAEDO: I will try to tell you everything from the beginning. On the days before as well, I and the others had always been in the habit of visiting Socrates. We would gather at dawn at the court where the trial had been held, for it was near the prison. Each day we would wait until the prison was opened, passing the time with one another, for it was not opened early; and when it was opened we would go in to Socrates and usually spend the day with him.

On that day we gathered earlier than usual; for the day before, when we came out of the prison in the evening, we learned that the ship had arrived from Delos. So we passed the word to one another to come as early as possible to the usual place. We came, and the doorkeeper, the one who usually answered, came out to us and told us to wait and not go in until he himself gave the word. The Eleven, he said, are taking the chains off Socrates and giving the order that he is to die today. After no long wait he came back and told us to go in.

When we went in we found Socrates just released from his chains, and Xanthippe — you know her — holding his little boy and sitting beside him. When Xanthippe saw us, she cried out and said the kind of thing women usually say: Socrates, this is the last time now that your friends will speak to you, and you to them.
And Socrates looked at Crito. Crito, he said, let someone take her home.

And some of Crito's people led her away, crying out and beating her breast. Socrates sat up on the couch, bent his leg and rubbed it hard with his hand, and as he rubbed it he said: What a strange thing it seems to be, gentlemen, this thing people call pleasant! How astonishingly it is related to what seems to be its opposite, the painful. The two are not willing to come to a person at the same time; yet if he pursues the one and catches it, he is almost always forced to catch the other too, as if they were fastened to a single head, though they are two. And I think, he said, that if Aesop had noticed them, he would have composed a story: that the god wanted to reconcile them when they were at war, and since he could not, he fastened their heads together, and that is why, when the one comes to anyone, the other follows afterward. And so it seems in my own case. Because of the chain there was the painful in my leg, and now the pleasant appears to have come following it.

Cebes took him up. By Zeus, Socrates, he said, you did well to remind me. About the poems you have composed, putting Aesop's tales into verse, and the hymn to Apollo, several others have already asked me, and Evenus asked just the other day, what you had in mind in composing them after you came here, when you had never composed anything before. So if you care at all that I should have an answer for Evenus when he asks me again — and I know very well he will ask — tell me what I should say.

Then tell him the truth, Cebes, he said: that I did not compose them wanting to be a rival to him or to his poems — I knew that would not be easy — but to test what certain dreams meant, and to acquit myself of a sacred duty, in case it was after all this kind of music that they were ordering me to make. They were something like this. The same dream came to me often in my past life, appearing in different shapes at different times but saying the same thing: Socrates, it said, make music and work at it. And in the time before, I took it to be urging and cheering me on to do the very thing I was doing: just as people cheer on runners, so the dream was cheering me on to do what I was doing, to make music, since philosophy is the greatest music and that was what I was doing.

But now, after the trial took place and the god's festival was keeping me from dying, I thought that, in case the dream was after all ordering me to make this music in the popular sense, I must not disobey it but make it; for it was safer not to go away before I had acquitted myself of the duty by composing poems in obedience to the dream. So first I composed one to the god whose festival was being kept. And after the god, reflecting that a poet, if he is going to be a poet, must compose stories and not arguments, and that I myself was no storyteller, for that reason I took the stories I had at hand and knew by heart, Aesop's, and put into verse the first of them I came upon. So tell Evenus this, Cebes, and tell him farewell, and, if he is sensible, to come after me as quickly as he can. I am going away, it seems, today; for the Athenians order it.

And Simmias said: What a thing to urge on Evenus, Socrates! I have met the man many times, and from what I have seen of him I would say he will not be willing to obey you in the least, if he can help it.
What? he said. Isn't Evenus a philosopher?
I think so, said Simmias.
Then Evenus will be willing, and so will everyone who has a worthy share in this pursuit. Perhaps, though, he will not do violence to himself; for they say that is not permitted.
And as he said this he lowered his legs to the ground, and sitting like that he carried on the rest of the conversation.
Then Cebes asked him: What do you mean by this, Socrates, that it is not permitted to do violence to oneself, and yet the philosopher would be willing to follow one who is dying?
What, Cebes? Haven't you and Simmias heard about such things, when you have been with Philolaus?
Nothing clear, Socrates.

Well, I too speak of them only from hearsay; but what I happen to have heard I do not grudge telling. And indeed it is perhaps most fitting of all for one who is about to travel there to examine the journey there and tell stories about it, what kind of thing we think it is. For what else could one do in the time until sunset?

Then on what ground do they say it is not permitted to kill oneself, Socrates? For I did hear from Philolaus before now, to answer what you asked just now, when he was living among us, and before now from some others too, that one must not do this. But I have never heard anything clear about it from anyone.

Well, you must keep trying, he said; for perhaps you may yet hear it. Perhaps, though, it will seem astonishing to you if this alone among all the rest is simple, and it never turns out for a human being, as it does in other things, that at some times and for some people it is better to be dead than to live. And for those for whom it is better to be dead, perhaps it seems astonishing to you if it is not holy for these people to do themselves the good turn, but they must wait for some other benefactor.
And Cebes laughed quietly. Zeus be witness, he said, speaking in his own dialect.

Yes, said Socrates, put that way it would seem unreasonable; and yet perhaps there is some reason in it. Now the account given of this in the secret teachings, that we human beings are in a kind of guard post and one must not release oneself from it or run away, seems to me a great one and not easy to see through. All the same, Cebes, this much seems to me well said: that it is gods who care for us, and that we human beings are one of the gods' possessions. Or do you not think so?
I do, said Cebes.
Then, he said, if one of your own possessions were to kill itself when you had given no sign that you wanted it dead, would you not be angry with it, and punish it if you had any punishment?
Certainly, he said.
Perhaps, then, in this way it is not unreasonable that one must not kill oneself before a god sends some necessity, like the one now upon us.

Well, that does seem likely, said Cebes. But what you were saying just now, that philosophers would readily be willing to die — that, Socrates, seems strange, if what we were saying just now is reasonable, that it is a god who cares for us and that we are his possessions. That the wisest should not resent leaving this care, in which those who oversee them are the best overseers there are, gods, makes no sense. For surely such a man does not think he will take better care of himself once he has become free. A person without sense might perhaps think so, that he ought to run away from his master; he would not reckon that one ought not to run away from a good master but stay with him as long as possible, and so he would run away without reckoning. But the one who has sense would desire, I suppose, always to be with one better than himself. And yet on this showing, Socrates, the opposite of what was said just now is likely: it is fitting for the wise to resent dying, and for the foolish to be glad.

When Socrates heard this he seemed to me to be pleased by the trouble Cebes took, and he looked at us and said: Cebes is always tracking down some argument or other, and he is not at all willing to be persuaded at once by whatever anyone says.

And Simmias said: But this time, Socrates, I think myself that there is something in what Cebes says. For why would men who are truly wise want to run away from masters better than themselves, and lightly be rid of them? And I think Cebes is aiming his argument at you, because you take it so lightly to leave both us and rulers who are good, as you yourself agree — gods.
What you both say is just, he said. I think you mean that I must make my defense against this as if in a court.
Very much so, said Simmias.

Come then, he said, let me try to make a more persuasive defense before you than I did before the judges. For I, he said, Simmias and Cebes, if I did not think that I was going first to other gods who are wise and good, and then to human beings who have died and are better than those here, would be doing wrong in not resenting death. But as it is, be sure that I hope to arrive among good men — though this I would not altogether insist on. But that I shall come to gods who are very good masters, be sure that if there is anything of this kind I would insist on, it is this. So for these reasons I do not resent it as I otherwise would, but am hopeful that there is something for those who have died, and, as has indeed been said from of old, something much better for the good than for the bad.

What then, Socrates? said Simmias. Do you have it in mind to go away keeping this thought to yourself, or would you share it with us too? For it seems to me that this is a good that belongs to us in common as well; and at the same time it will be your defense, if you persuade us of what you say.
I will try, he said. But first let us find out from Crito here what it is that he has, I think, been wanting to say for some time.

Only this, Socrates, said Crito: the man who is going to give you the poison has been telling me for some time that I must tell you to talk as little as possible. He says that people get more heated when they talk, and that one must bring nothing of that kind to the poison; otherwise those who do so are sometimes forced to drink twice or even three times.
And Socrates said: Never mind him. Just let him see to his own part and be ready to give it twice, and if need be three times.
I pretty well knew that, said Crito; but he has been pestering me for some time.

Let him be, he said. But to you, the judges, I now want to render my account: how it appears to me reasonable that a man who has really spent his life in philosophy should be confident when he is about to die, and hopeful that he will win the greatest goods there when he has died. How this could be so, Simmias and Cebes, I will try to tell you.

It is likely that those who happen to take hold of philosophy in the right way have escaped the notice of other people in this: that they themselves practice nothing else but dying and being dead. Now if this is true, it would surely be strange for them to be eager all their lives for nothing but this, and then, when it comes, to resent the very thing they had long been eager for and practicing.

And Simmias laughed. By Zeus, Socrates, he said, I was in no mood for laughing just now, but you have made me laugh. For I think that most people, hearing this very thing, would think it very well said against those who practice philosophy — and the people in our country would agree entirely — that those who practice philosophy really are longing for death, and that it has not escaped them that this is what philosophers deserve to suffer.

And they would be telling the truth, Simmias, except for its not having escaped them. For it has escaped them in what way true philosophers long for death, and in what way they deserve death, and what kind of death. Let us speak among ourselves, then, he said, and say goodbye to them. Do we think that death is something?
Certainly, said Simmias in reply.

Is it anything other than the parting of the soul from the body? And is this what being dead is: the body, parted from the soul, has come to be apart, itself by itself, and the soul, parted from the body, is apart, itself by itself? Is death anything other than this?
No, just this, he said.

Then consider, my good man, whether you think as I do; for from these things, I think, we shall know more about what we are examining. Does it appear to you to belong to a philosopher to be in earnest about the so-called pleasures of this sort — those of food and drink, for instance?
Least of all, Socrates, said Simmias.
And the pleasures of sex?
Not at all.

And the other attentions paid to the body? Do you think such a man holds them in honor? Getting fine cloaks and sandals, for instance, and the other adornments of the body — do you think he honors them or despises them, except so far as it is quite necessary to have a share in them?
I think he despises them, he said, the true philosopher at least.
Then in general, he said, do you think such a man's concern is not with the body, but that so far as he can he stands away from it and is turned toward the soul?
I do.
Then first of all, in such things it is clear that the philosopher releases his soul as far as possible from its partnership with the body, beyond all other people?
It appears so.

And most people, I suppose, Simmias, think that for one who finds nothing of this sort pleasant and has no share in it, life is not worth living, and that he who gives no thought to the pleasures that come through the body comes pretty close to being dead.
That's very true.

And what about the getting of wisdom itself? Is the body a hindrance or not, if one takes it along as a partner in the search? I mean something like this: do sight and hearing hold any truth for human beings, or is it as even the poets are always dinning into us, that we neither hear nor see anything exactly? And yet if these among the senses of the body are not exact or clear, the others will hardly be; for they are all, I suppose, poorer than these. Or do you not think so?
Very much so, he said.
When, then, he said, does the soul lay hold of the truth? For whenever it tries to examine anything together with the body, clearly it is then deceived by it.
That's true.
Then is it not in reasoning, if anywhere, that any of the things that are becomes plain to it?
Yes.

And it reasons best, I suppose, when none of these things troubles it, neither hearing nor sight nor pain nor any pleasure, but it comes to be as far as possible itself by itself, letting the body go, and, so far as it can, having no partnership or contact with it, reaches out for what is.
That is so.
Then here too the philosopher's soul most despises the body and flees from it, and seeks to come to be itself by itself?
It appears so.
And what about things like these, Simmias? Do we say that the just itself is something, or nothing?
We do say so, by Zeus.
And again the beautiful, and the good?
Of course.
Well, have you ever yet seen any such thing with your eyes?
Not at all, he said.

Or have you laid hold of them by any other of the senses that work through the body? I am speaking of all of them — largeness, for instance, health, strength, and in a word the being of all the rest, what each one actually is. Is what is truest in them beheld through the body? Or is it like this: whoever of us prepares himself most fully and most exactly to think of each thing he examines, itself, will come nearest to knowing each?
Very much so.

Then would he do this most purely who goes to each thing as far as possible with thought itself, not setting any sight beside his thinking, nor dragging in any other sense at all along with his reasoning? He would use thought itself by itself, unmixed, and try to hunt down each of the things that are, itself by itself, unmixed, rid as far as possible of eyes and ears and, so to speak, of the whole body, because it confuses the soul and does not let it get truth and wisdom whenever it is its partner. Is this not the man, Simmias, if anyone, who will reach what is?
What you say is extraordinarily true, Socrates, said Simmias.

Then from all this, he said, some such belief as the following must come to those who are genuinely philosophers, so that they say such things as these to one another too: It looks as if a kind of path is bringing us out, with the argument beside us in our inquiry, to this: as long as we have the body, and our soul is kneaded together with an evil of this kind, we shall never sufficiently get what we desire; and that, we say, is the truth. For the body keeps us busy in countless ways because of the food it must have; and besides, if any diseases fall on us, they hinder our hunt for what is. It fills us with loves and desires and fears and phantoms of every kind and a great deal of nonsense, so that, as the saying goes, truly and really, because of it we never get to think anything at all. For wars and factions and battles come from nothing else but the body and its desires. All wars arise over the getting of money, and we are forced to get money because of the body, as slaves in its service; and from this, because of all these things, we have no leisure for philosophy. And the last thing of all is that if we do get some leisure from it and turn to examining something, in our searches again it bursts in everywhere, making an uproar and confusion and stunning us, so that because of it we cannot see the truth.

No, it has really been shown to us that if we are ever going to know anything purely, we must be rid of it and behold the things themselves with the soul itself. And then, it seems, we shall have what we desire and say we are lovers of, wisdom: when we have died, as the argument indicates, and not while we live. For if it is not possible to know anything purely in company with the body, then one of two things: either knowledge can be got nowhere, or only by those who have died; for then the soul will be itself by itself, apart from the body, and not before. And in the time we are alive we shall be nearest to knowing, it seems, in this way: if as far as possible we have no dealings and no partnership with the body, beyond what is entirely necessary, and do not fill ourselves with its nature, but keep ourselves pure of it until the god himself releases us. And being pure in this way, rid of the body's foolishness, we shall in all likelihood be with others of that kind, and shall know through our own selves all that is unmixed; and this, perhaps, is the truth. For it may be that it is not permitted for the impure to lay hold of the pure.
Such things, Simmias, I think all who love learning in the right way must say to one another and believe. Or do you not think so?
More than anything, Socrates.

Then, said Socrates, if this is true, my friend, there is great hope that one who arrives where I am traveling will there, if anywhere, sufficiently get the thing for which we have taken so much trouble in our past life. So the journey now appointed for me comes with good hope, and so it does for any other man who believes that his thought has been made ready, purified as it were.
Very much so, said Simmias.

And does purification not turn out to be this, as has been said in the argument for some time: separating the soul as far as possible from the body, and accustoming it to gather and collect itself, by itself, from every part of the body, and to dwell, so far as it can, both in the present and in the time to come, alone by itself, released from the body as if from chains?
Very much so, he said.
Then this is what is named death, a release and separation of soul from body?
Entirely so, he said.

And those who are always most eager to release it, as we say, and the only ones, are those who practice philosophy in the right way; and the practice of philosophers is just this, a release and separation of soul from body. Or is it not?
It appears so.
Then, as I said at the beginning, it would be ridiculous for a man to prepare himself in life to live as near as he can to being dead, and then, when it comes to him, to resent it?
Ridiculous, of course.

In truth, then, Simmias, he said, those who practice philosophy in the right way are practicing dying, and being dead is less fearful to them than to anyone else in the world. Consider it from this. If they are at odds with the body in every way and desire to have the soul itself by itself, and then, when this happens, they were to be afraid and resent it, would that not be very unreasonable — if they did not go gladly to the place where, on arriving, they may hope to get what they loved all through life, and what they loved was wisdom, and to be rid of the company of what they were at odds with? When human loves and wives and sons have died, many have been willing to go after them to Hades of their own accord, led by this hope, of seeing there those they longed for and being with them. And will someone who is really in love with wisdom, and has firmly taken hold of this same hope, that he will meet it nowhere else in any way worth speaking of but in Hades, resent dying and not go there gladly? One must think he will go gladly, my friend, if he really is a philosopher; for he will firmly believe this, that nowhere else but there will he meet wisdom purely. And if this is so, as I was just saying, would it not be very unreasonable if such a man feared death?
Very, by Zeus, he said.

Then is this proof enough for you, he said, about a man whom you see resenting that he is about to die, that he was not after all a lover of wisdom but a lover of the body? And this same man, I suppose, is also a lover of money and a lover of honor, either one of these or both.
It is very much as you say, he said.
Then, Simmias, he said, does not what is named courage also belong most of all to those who are so disposed?
Surely, he said.

And self-command too, what even the many name self-command — not being in a flutter about the desires, but making little of them and staying orderly — does this not belong only to those who most of all make little of the body and live in philosophy?
It must be, he said.
For if you are willing, he said, to consider the courage and self-command of the others, they will seem to you strange.
How so, Socrates?
You know, he said, that all the others count death among the great evils?
Indeed they do, he said.
Then is it from fear of greater evils that the brave among them face death, when they do face it?
That is so.
Then it is by being afraid, and by fear, that all are brave except the philosophers. And yet it is unreasonable for anyone to be brave by fear and cowardice.
Very much so.

And what of the orderly among them? Has not this same thing happened to them: they are self-commanded by a kind of self-indulgence? And yet we say that is impossible; but all the same, what happens to them with this simple-minded self-command turns out to be like that. For because they fear to be deprived of other pleasures, and desire those, they keep away from some because they are mastered by others. And yet they call it self-indulgence to be ruled by pleasures; but all the same it turns out that they master some pleasures because they are mastered by other pleasures. And this is like what was said just now, that in a way they have been made self-commanded through self-indulgence.
Yes, so it seems.

My dear Simmias, I fear this is not the right exchange for virtue, to trade pleasures for pleasures and pains for pains and fear for fear, and greater for lesser, like coins. I fear that the only right coin, for which all these must be traded, is wisdom; and that everything bought and sold for this and with this is really courage and self-command and justice and, in a word, true virtue, together with wisdom, whether pleasures and fears and all other things of that kind are added or taken away. But when they are separated from wisdom and exchanged for one another, I fear that virtue of that kind is a sort of painted shadow, and is really fit for slaves, and has nothing sound or true in it; and that in truth self-command and justice and courage are a kind of purification from all such things, and wisdom itself is a kind of purifying rite.

And it may be that those who established the rites for us were no fools, but have really been speaking in riddles all along when they say that whoever arrives in Hades uninitiated and without the rites will lie in mud, while the one who arrives there purified and with the rites completed will dwell with gods. For there are indeed, as those concerned with the rites say, ‘many who carry the wand, but few who are Bacchants.’ And these, in my belief, are none other than those who have practiced philosophy in the right way. I too, so far as I could, have left nothing undone in my life to become one of them, but have been eager for it in every way. Whether I was eager in the right way, and whether we accomplished anything, we shall know for certain when we get there, if a god wills, a little later, as I think.

This then, he said, Simmias and Cebes, is my defense: that it is reasonable for me to leave you and my masters here without taking it hard or resenting it, since I believe that there too, no less than here, I shall meet good masters and good companions. Most people do not believe this. So if I am any more persuasive to you in my defense than I was to the judges of the Athenians, it would be well.

divergences.phrase: ὡς ἔν τινι φρουρᾷ ἐσμεν οἱ ἄνθρωποι καὶ οὐ δεῖ δὴ ἑαυτὸν ἐκ ταύτης λύειν οὐδ’ ἀποδιδράσκειν
divergences.older: man is a prisoner who has no right to open the door and run away
divergences.lectio: we human beings are in a kind of guard post and one must not release oneself from it or run away
divergences.note: Phroura can mean a prison or a garrison where a soldier stands watch, and Plato leaves it open with 'a kind of'. Jowett settles it as a prison and adds a door; the edition keeps the one word and adds nothing.

divergences.phrase: οὐδὲν ἄλλο αὐτοὶ ἐπιτηδεύουσιν ἢ ἀποθνῄσκειν τε καὶ τεθνάναι
divergences.older: he is always pursuing death and dying
divergences.lectio: they themselves practice nothing else but dying and being dead
divergences.note: The Greek has two verbs, the act of dying and the state of being dead, and a word for a practice or occupation, not a chase. The whole defense turns on that practice, so it is named here as it is at 67e and later at 81a.

divergences.phrase: ἕως ἂν ὁ θεὸς αὐτὸς ἀπολύσῃ ἡμᾶς
divergences.older: until the hour when God himself is pleased to release us
divergences.lectio: until the god himself releases us
divergences.note: Jowett's capital and his 'is pleased' make the line sound like a Christian prayer. Plato writes 'the god', as he does throughout these dialogues, and a bare verb; it answers 62c, where one must not kill oneself before a god sends some necessity.
